meta.title: The spread of printing, 1454–1500
meta.description: The first press in each of 57 towns, placed where and when it began. Each link says where the printer came from: the shop he trained in, the type he used, or the town he moved on from.
sources: Incunabula Short Title Catalogue (ISTC), British Library / CERL
L. Febvre and H.-J. Martin, The Coming of the Book (1958; Eng. tr. 1976), appendix on the spread of printing
Dates and printers cross-checked by web search on 25 Sept 2026; see SOURCE.md
meta.caveats: Each town is dated by its first dated or securely datable print, so a press may have begun a year earlier. Links in grey are inference: where a printer trained or came from is recorded for only some towns, and the rest are joined to the nearest earlier press on a plausible route until the record is checked. Places are the town, not the shop. The whole set is awaiting a line-by-line check against the ISTC.

linkKinds.training: the printer learned the craft there
linkKinds.copy: type or method taken from there
linkKinds.move: the same printer moved on from there
linkKinds.influence: shaped by, without training or type

nodes.label: Mainz
nodes.note: Johann Gutenberg. The 1454–55 indulgences and the 42-line Bible; Fust and Schoeffer carry the shop on after 1455.

nodes.label: Strasbourg
nodes.note: Johann Mentelin. A Latin Bible finished no later than 1460. Where he learned to print is not recorded.

nodes.label: Bamberg
nodes.note: Albrecht Pfister. His first dated book is of 1461; the 36-line Bible, in a type first used by Gutenberg, is probably a little earlier.

nodes.label: Subiaco
nodes.place: Benedictine abbey of Santa Scolastica, Subiaco
nodes.note: Konrad Sweynheym and Arnold Pannartz, the first press in Italy. Sweynheym is thought to have worked for Fust and Schoeffer in Mainz.

nodes.label: Cologne
nodes.note: Ulrich Zell, a cleric of the Mainz diocese who learned the art there; the 1499 Cologne Chronicle names him as its source on Gutenberg.

nodes.label: Eltville
nodes.note: The Bechtermünze brothers, printing the Vocabularius ex quo in type from Gutenberg's shop.

nodes.label: Rome
nodes.note: Sweynheym and Pannartz move here from Subiaco; Ulrich Han prints in Rome the same year.

nodes.label: Basel
nodes.note: Berthold Ruppel, named as a member of Gutenberg's household in the 1455 Helmasperger notarial instrument. Some sources date his first work to 1467.

nodes.label: Augsburg
nodes.note: Günther Zainer, who probably learned in Strasbourg.

nodes.label: Venice
nodes.note: Johannes de Spira (Johann of Speyer), granted a five-year monopoly on printing in Venice; Nicolas Jenson follows in 1470.

nodes.label: Nuremberg
nodes.note: Johann Sensenschmidt; Anton Koberger from 1471.

nodes.label: Foligno
nodes.note: Johann Neumeister, who printed the first edition of Dante's Commedia here in 1472.

nodes.label: Paris
nodes.note: Ulrich Gering, Michael Friburger and Martin Crantz, brought to the Sorbonne by Guillaume Fichet and Johann Heynlin; Heynlin had studied at Basel.

nodes.label: Milan
nodes.note: Antonio Zarotto and Philippus de Lavagnia; an earlier start in 1469 is claimed but not proven.

nodes.label: Beromünster
nodes.note: Helias Helye, canon of the collegiate church. The Mammotrectus, finished 10 November 1470, is the first dated book printed in Switzerland.

nodes.label: Naples
nodes.note: Sixtus Riessinger, a priest from Strasbourg.

nodes.label: Florence
nodes.note: Bernardo Cennini, a goldsmith who is said to have worked out the method for himself.

nodes.label: Bologna
nodes.note: Balthasar Azoguidus.

nodes.label: Ferrara
nodes.note: André Belfort, a Frenchman.

nodes.label: Treviso
nodes.note: Gerardus de Lisa.

nodes.label: Speyer
nodes.note: Peter Drach.

nodes.label: Verona
nodes.note: Johannes of Verona.

nodes.label: Padua
nodes.note: Bartholomaeus de Valdezoccho and Martinus de Septem Arboribus.

nodes.label: Segovia
nodes.note: Johannes Párix, a German printer hired in Rome by the Bishop of Segovia: the Sinodal de Aguilafuente, the first book printed in Spain.

nodes.label: Ulm
nodes.note: Johann Zainer, a kinsman of Günther Zainer of Augsburg, from Strasbourg.

nodes.label: Buda
nodes.note: Andreas Hess, invited from Georg Lauer's printing house in Rome: the Chronica Hungarorum, finished 5 June 1473, the first book printed in Hungary.

nodes.label: Kraków
nodes.note: Kasper Straube, an itinerant printer from Bavaria; the almanac for 1474, printed in 1473, is the oldest known print from Poland.

nodes.label: Lyon
nodes.note: Guillaume Le Roy of Liège, backed by the merchant Barthélemy Buyer; his first dated book is of 17 September 1473.

nodes.label: Utrecht
nodes.note: Nicolaus Ketelaer and Gerardus de Leempt: the Historia scholastica, the earliest dated book printed in the Low Countries.

nodes.label: Aalst
nodes.note: Dirk Martens, with Johannes de Westfalia; Martens is said to have learned printing in Venice.

nodes.label: Valencia
nodes.note: Lambert Palmart. Obres o trobes en lahors de la Verge Maria, 1474; some sources place the first press in 1473.

nodes.label: Leuven
nodes.note: Johannes de Westfalia moves here from Aalst.

nodes.label: Vicenza
nodes.note: Leonardus Achates.

nodes.label: Bruges
nodes.note: William Caxton and Colard Mansion: The Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye, the first book printed in English. Caxton had learned to print in Cologne in 1471–72.

nodes.label: Lübeck
nodes.note: Lucas Brandis: the Rudimentum novitiorum.

nodes.label: Zaragoza
nodes.note: Matthew Flander and German printers.

nodes.label: Toulouse
nodes.note: A Repetitio on Roman law dated 21 June 1476; printing there may have begun in 1475.

nodes.label: Angers
nodes.note: Jean de La Tour and Jean Morel.

nodes.label: Westminster
nodes.note: William Caxton sets up at Westminster Abbey after Bruges: the first press in England.

nodes.label: Plzeň
nodes.note: The first dated Czech print; the Trojan Chronicle may be earlier.

nodes.label: Seville
nodes.note: Antonio Martínez, Bartolomé Segura and Alfonso del Puerto.

nodes.label: Gouda
nodes.note: Gerard Leeu.

nodes.label: Deventer
nodes.note: Richard Pafraet.

nodes.label: Delft
nodes.note: Jacob Jacobszoon van der Meer and Mauricius Yemantszoon: the Delft Bible, the first Bible printed in Dutch.

nodes.label: Oxford
nodes.note: Theoderic Rood of Cologne, who seems to have brought his press from there. His first book is dated 17 December 1478, misprinted as 1468.

nodes.label: Geneva
nodes.note: Adam Steinschaber.

nodes.label: St Albans
nodes.note: The anonymous Schoolmaster Printer.

nodes.label: London
nodes.note: John Lettou, joined by William de Machlinia.

nodes.label: Salamanca
nodes.note: An anonymous press serving the university.

nodes.label: Antwerp
nodes.note: Mathias van der Goes; Gerard Leeu moves here from Gouda in 1484.

nodes.label: Leipzig
nodes.note: Marcus Brandis, of the Brandis family of printers.

nodes.label: Vienna
nodes.note: A Vocabolista of 1482, possibly printed by Stephan Koblinger, who had printed in Vicenza in 1479–80. The attribution is uncertain.

nodes.label: Odense
nodes.note: Johann Snell, brought by Bishop Karl Rønnow to print the Breviarium Ottoniense, the first book printed in Denmark.

nodes.label: Stockholm
nodes.note: Johann Snell again: the Dialogus creaturarum, the first book printed in Sweden.

nodes.label: Faro
nodes.note: Samuel Gacon: a Hebrew Pentateuch finished 30 June 1487, the first book printed in Portugal.

nodes.label: Lisbon
nodes.note: Eliezer Toledano, printing in Hebrew.

nodes.label: Cetinje
nodes.note: Hieromonk Makarije, sent to Venice to learn printing: the Octoechos of the First Tone, finished 4 January 1494, the first book printed in Cyrillic among the South Slavs.
